title: Tŷ Mawr — The Great House Farm Story

acts.label: Prologue
acts.title: The Root
acts.logline: Before the farm is ever divided, its title has a root: the church, the manor, the Vaughans, the Bute Estate.

acts.label: Act I
acts.title: The Split
acts.logline: 1877: the house goes one way and the fields another. Two parcels, two owners, two chains of title.

acts.label: Act II
acts.title: Two Words
acts.logline: "The whole farm." A tenancy describes two parcels as one, just as the house becomes the family's own.

acts.label: Act III
acts.title: The Mimic
acts.logline: The deeds vanish. Then, one move at a time, a second Parcel A is built on paper out of tenancies and court orders.

acts.label: Act IV
acts.title: The Handover
acts.logline: BP takes the fields by deed and the mimic by order, licence and conveyance. Then it registers both.

acts.label: Act V
acts.title: Possession, Not Ownership
acts.logline: The mimic is folded into the fields, and the courts decide who may live in the house. Never who owns it.

acts.label: Act VI
acts.title: Bulldozed Before Breakfast
acts.logline: A chainsaw at the door, a forced eviction, a listing refused, and bulldozers at 4am.

acts.label: Act VII
acts.title: Built Over
acts.logline: BP sells the merged title, twenty houses go up, and a thousand graves are taken out of the ground.

acts.label: Act VIII
acts.title: The Buried Title
acts.logline: Mary's grandchildren dig for the true Parcel A. The state says its register is correct.

acts.label: Epilogue
acts.title: Today
acts.logline: How it was done, who holds what, and what was never decided.

scenes.title: The church beside the house
scenes.narration: Long before there is a farm, there is a church. St Dochdwy's at Llandough is one of the oldest Christian sites in Wales, the seat of an early monastery. Beside it, on the slope above the river, stands the place that will become Tŷ Mawr: the Great House. This is a story about who owns that ground, and how the answer was buried.

scenes.title: An old house
scenes.narration: In the Middle Ages people live and work on this slope; their pottery is still in the ground eight hundred years later. The house that grows here is old and grand: a long stone house the Royal Commission will judge sub-medieval, probably of the seventeenth century, perhaps built around something older still.

scenes.title: Cydfin, or Tŷ Mawr
scenes.narration: In the manor's leases it goes by an older name: Cydfin, or Tŷ Mawr, a farm of a hundred and seven acres. Every lease is written, signed and kept. Remember that. For three centuries this land's paper trail is unbroken.

scenes.title: The Vaughans of Great House
scenes.narration: The title has a root. A letter to the Western Mail will one day trace it from Tewkesbury Abbey to the Crown and the Herberts. From the middle of the sixteenth century the Vaughans, a minor gentry family, hold Great House as the chief freehold farm of the parish. Their memorials are still in the church next door.

evidence.title: Western Mail, 'Grievous loss' (letter tracing the descent)

scenes.title: The Williamses arrive
scenes.narration: In 1667 the Williams family come to Great House. Mary Williams, born there two and a half centuries later, will say her ancestors bought it. From now on, for more than three hundred years, there is a Williams in the house.

scenes.title: The Marquesses of Bute
scenes.narration: Early in the nineteenth century the Bute Estate, the greatest landowner in South Wales, takes the freehold. The manor courts of Llandough and Leckwith sit in the house itself. By 1818 Llandough's rents are in Bute's books, and in 1824 the estate's surveyor walks the farm and writes it down. One owner, one farm, one title.

scenes.title: The Great House shrinks
scenes.narration: Then, on paper, the Great House begins to shrink. In the census and the tithe returns it stops being 'Great House' and becomes 'Great House Farm': no longer the court house of a manor, just a farmhouse. It is the first time the records describe the place as something less than it is. In this story, how a thing is described will matter as much as what it is.

scenes.title: Bones by the church
scenes.narration: Workmen digging foundations beside the church find six skeletons, a medieval spearhead and a spur. The bones are put back in the ground by the churchyard stile. Llandough's dead lie close under the surface. Nobody yet asks how many there are.

scenes.title: The soldier under the floor
scenes.narration: Under the dining-room floor of the Great House, the family will always say, lies a soldier in armour, with his horse, his lance and a small shield. The story is told for a hundred years. It reaches the Daily Telegraph and the Royal Commission's files. Nobody ever lifts the floor to look.

scenes.title: The quarrymen
scenes.narration: Limestone brings the quarrymen. The Bute Estate lets about thirty-three acres of the farm to the Llandough Limeworks, and for the next thirty-five years the quarry eats into the land.

scenes.title: The split
scenes.narration: 1877. The move that everything turns on. The Bute Estate sells the farmhouse, its buildings and about ten acres to the quarryman Daniel Thomas. Call it Parcel A. Bute keeps nine acres of fields on the top. Call that Parcel B. From today they are two pieces of land with two owners and two chains of title. The Williamses stay on as tenants of both: of the house under Thomas, of the fields under Bute. And, as Mary will tell it, with a promise: when the quarrying ends, the freehold of the house comes to them. Hold on to this. Bute no longer owns the house. Anything Bute sells after today can only be Parcel B.

scenes.title: "The whole farm"
scenes.narration: February 1916. Bute lets John Williams "the whole farm" on a yearly tenancy. Read those words with what we now know. Bute has not owned the house since 1877. It owns the fields, Parcel B, and nothing else here. So "the whole farm" is a landlord describing land it does not own as if it did. The words are Bute's, not the family's. The tenancy itself has never been found; only those three words survive, quoted seventy years later by the Court of Appeal as the start of the story. From here on there are two Great House Farms: the real one, in two parcels, and a mythical one, a single estate that exists only on paper. Call it the synthetic farm. Every case against the family will be fought over the synthetic farm.

scenes.narration: In 1928 the last of the quarry machinery leaves. John Williams pays a final rent of about four pounds to Alfred Thomas, and the bargain of 1877 comes due: the quarrying is over, and the freehold of the house passes to the family. Mary sees the receipt. From this year the true Parcel A has a complete chain: the Vaughans, Bute, Daniel Thomas, the Williamses. The family pay no more rent on the house, to anyone, ever again.

It has no deed to the house, and it never will.

scenes.title: Twelve years
scenes.narration: By 1940 the Williamses, John and his daughter Mary in the house, have lived there twelve years without paying anyone a penny for it. In law, twelve years is enough. Even without a single paper, there is from now on no basis for anyone to call Mary's occupation of her house permissive. Everything that follows has to pretend this year never happened.

scenes.title: Nothing in writing
scenes.narration: February 1949. John Williams gives up his tenancy of the fields, and Frederick takes them on from Western Ground Rents. Nothing is written down: no lease, no plan. And now the first attempt to make Mary's occupation look permissive: the landlord begins to speak of Frederick's fields tenancy as a tenancy of "the farm", house and all, as if the house were his and she lived there by his tenancy. Mary rejects it. The house is hers, it was never in any tenancy of the fields, and she has the paper title in the blanket box to prove it. Note who blurs the two parcels here. Not the family. The landlord's own 1939 plan shows it knew exactly where the line was.

scenes.narration: 1950. An estate agent from Penarth places a lodger in the farmhouse. He stays two years. Before he goes, he tells Mary what he has done: he has taken the papers from the family's blanket box, 'including the agreement relating to the farm', and handed them to the agent. Mary will say she believed it was connected with the landlord's first move against the farm, which comes within three years. Think about what it means. The true Parcel A still exists, and its chain is still complete. But the paper that proves it has left the house a year after she produced it as her answer. From now on, every time Mary says 'the house is mine', she will be asked for documents she no longer has.

scenes.title: The first order
scenes.narration: February 1955. Western Ground Rents sues Frederick, its tenant of the fields, and gets a High Court order for possession of "the whole of the farm". Now unpack it. The tenancy that ended was a tenancy of the fields. The landlord was the owner of the fields. An order giving a landlord back what it let can only reach Parcel B. "The whole of the farm" is the synthetic farm again: borrowed words that reach over the house without the landlord ever proving a right to it. Mary, who owns the house, is not a party and is never heard. On 4 July the order is enforced. The fields are taken. The family's account is that the woodland on the north side of Parcel A goes too, to a couple in Llandough, and later to a charity that has never touched it. The house is left: Mary, just home from hospital after losing a leg, stands her ground. Years later this order will be read as the day a twelve-year clock started running on her house. It wasn't. Whatever clock started in 1955 was a clock on the fields. The second attempt to make Mary's occupation look permissive is an insinuation, and it will later be mistaken for a fact.

scenes.title: Mary says no
scenes.narration: The third attempt. In 1959 Western Ground Rents offers Mary a tenancy of "the farmhouse and garden", on their own. Notice the words. Not "the farm" this time. The landlord names the house parcel by itself: Parcel A, less the woodland to the north and the land to the south already being taken from around it. It knows exactly which piece is separate, and exactly which piece it has no deed to. Why else offer a tenancy of a house you say you own? If she signs, she becomes a tenant, and a tenant's occupation is permissive by definition. She refuses. The house is hers, she tells them, through her grandfather, and there are documents to prove it. The documents are in someone else's hands. The court will one day record that they were "never produced".

scenes.title: The 1962 order
scenes.narration: The fourth attempt, and the one that will matter most. 11 December 1962: in Cardiff County Court, Judge Temple Morris QC orders Frederick and Mary out of "the farmhouse and garden", and to pay for every year back to 1955. Again the house parcel, named on its own. For the first time Mary is a party. But this is a possession order, not a ruling on title. It treats her as someone holding over on the old "whole farm" tenancy, a permitted occupier who has outstayed her welcome, when she was never in that tenancy at all. Western Ground Rents proves no deed to the house, because it has none. And then it does nothing. The order is never carried out. It goes into a drawer. Twenty-five years from now, it is what will save BP's case.

scenes.narration: The fifth attempt. 2 March 1965: the agents offer 'Mrs Williams' a weekly tenancy of the farmhouse and garden at two pounds a week. An owner who holds the deed to a house does not need to fold it into someone else's tenancy, word an order against the wrong tenant, offer the occupier a tenancy, then another. An owner sues on its deed. Western Ground Rents never once did.

scenes.title: The handover
scenes.narration: 31 December 1969. Western Ground Rents sells out to the BP Pension Trust, the pension fund of British Petroleum. The conveyance speaks of "Great House Farm", one estate: the synthetic farm passes one more time in a single phrase. Look at what can actually pass. Parcel B, the fields, passes with a proper chain: Bute, Western Ground Rents, BP. For the house, Western Ground Rents has no deed to hand over. What it has is a case: the 1962 order, the refused tenancies, the "whole farm" wording. That is what BP takes on for Parcel A: not the house, but the claim against it. This conveyance will later be recited as the root of BP's title. Today it is missing from the Land Registry's files.

The development needs the house. The house needs a title.

scenes.title: The Court of Appeal
scenes.narration: 31 July 1987, the Court of Appeal. Here is the twist. The judges find that Frederick and Mary were in adverse possession of the house from 1955. The clock was running against the landlord. So why does BP win? Because of two of the attempts. The 1962 order, never enforced, was brought within twelve years and so stopped the clock. A conveyance they themselves call "the actual conveyance of the farmhouse and garden": a separate deed for the house. Count from 1928, as the house's own history requires, and the twelve years were up in 1940, fifteen years before any order. Mary's title documents, the judgment notes, were "never produced". Nobody asks where they went. BP is recorded as having "the paper title to the farm": paper to the fields, and for the house only a deed between two BP companies. BP Properties Ltd v Buckler goes into the law books as a leading case on adverse possession. It decided possession. It never decided ownership.

scenes.title: How it was done
scenes.narration: So here is how it was done. Not with one forged deed, but with a sequence. First, two words in 1916 made two parcels one farm, in a landlord's document, never the family's. Then six attempts to make Mary's occupation of her own house look permissive: her house spoken of as part of her husband's fields tenancy; an order against the fields tenant worded for the whole farm; a tenancy offered, and refused; a possession order made and left in a drawer; another tenancy offered, and refused; and a licence she never asked for and never accepted. Alongside them, the woodland and the land to the south were taken from around her. Then the paper: BP took the fields by deed and the case against the house with them; one BP company conveyed the house to another; the state registered it, then folded it into the fields. The family, for their part, were led into claiming adverse possession of the mythical farm, counted from an order about the fields, when Parcel A had been theirs since 1928 and by possession since 1940. And the courts, asked only who had the right to possession, never had to ask who owned the house. In English law, possession can be awarded without ownership ever being tried, and a title can be registered without any court deciding a rival claim to the same land. Neither step, on its own, decides the older title. Every move went through one of those two doors.

scenes.title: Who knew
scenes.narration: So who knew the farm was two? Mary did, in her way. Her 1974 statement tells of the house and ten acres sold to Daniel Thomas, and the nine acres Bute kept. But her deeds were gone, and no lawyer of hers ever turned that history into a case about two parcels. If the family had grasped what it meant, they would have shouted it from the rooftops; it was their whole case. The other side never needed it explained. Western Ground Rents offered tenancies of "the farmhouse and garden" alone, and sued for it alone. BP conveyed it alone, between its own companies, registered it alone, and then merged it. The Land Registry issued two titles and joined them into one. The Court of Appeal read a conveyance of "the farmhouse and garden". Everyone made a mess of this case: the drafting, the lawyers, the courts, the Registry. A haze over the two parcels might be forgiven once. But the people who knew best treated the two parcels as one whenever that helped, and as two whenever that helped more. The family call it what it looks like: a conspiracy against them.
